processing: The fruiting spikes are gathered in summer as they dry on the plant and are sun-dried; in Taiwan the whole herb is often used. They are then simmered in water.
harvest_season: Summer, once the flower spikes have finished and begun to wither.
appearance_dry: Dry, dark brown, papery spikes a few centimetres long.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear amber to mid brown, darker with a longer boil.
appearance_wet: Softened brown spikes with overlapping bracts.
taste_profile: Described in Chinese medicine as pungent and bitter, yet in Japan valued as an easy herbal tea with little strong character; shop versions are often sweetened.

brewing.notes: The Japanese folk method is 5 to 10 g simmered in 400 to 600 ml until reduced by half. Keep it occasional, not daily.

vintage_note: Not sold by year: it is a dried herb from herbal shops, or a ready drink at liangcha counters. Buy the most recent crop you can find, with intact spikes and no musty smell.
description:
Xia ku cao is the Chinese name for self-heal, Prunella vulgaris, a small plant of the mint family that grows across Asia, Europe, Africa and North America. The name means summer-withered herb, because the plant dies back after the summer solstice.

The part used is the dried flower spike. Liangcha shops in southern China sell the drink ready-made, and it is an ingredient in Xia Sang Ju and in the Wong Lo Kat formula.

On its own it is plain and herbal with some bitterness; many shop versions are sweetened. Simmer rather than steep it, since these are tough, dry spikes.

Do not drink it casually in quantity. Chinese medicine classes it as cold, and animal studies have linked extracts to immune suppression and raised liver enzymes. Those are not human trials, but they are reason for moderation, and for asking a doctor if you take medication or are pregnant.
history:
The herb appears in Li Shizhen's Compendium of Materia Medica under names such as tie se cao, nai dong and yan mian. It is also in the Japanese Pharmacopoeia as kagoso, and most of what Japan sells comes from China.

Outside China, Indigenous peoples of North America had their own uses: the Nuxalk boiled the plant into a weak tea and the Nlaka'pamux drank a cold infusion. Its large role in modern drinks comes through southern Chinese herbal teas; adding it to the Wanglaoji formula was approved after animal testing in 2005.
